A.q: People with which of the following learning styles learn better when information is presented in a picture format?
options: Auditory
Kinesthetic
Non-Verbal – Visual
Verbal – Visual
A.explain: Non-verbal visual learners learn from picture format — videos, maps, charts, diagrams. Verbal-visual learners prefer written words.

A.q: Which learning style generally prefers pictures, diagrams, maps, and demonstrations?
options: Kinesthetic
Auditory
Olfactory
Visual
A.explain: Visual learners prefer to see information: pictures, diagrams, cartoons, maps, and demonstrations.

A.q: Which activity best supports a kinesthetic learner?
options: Memorizing diagrams without interaction
Avoiding movement while studying
Completing hands-on activities
Listening to a lecture without taking action
A.explain: Hands-on work — touching, building, moving, acting out — supports kinesthetic learning.

A.q: According to the lecture, which group includes most people?
options: Most people are auditory learners
Most people are visual learners
Most people are purely kinesthetic learners
Most people have no identifiable style
A.explain: The lecture states most people are visual learners.

A.q: Is chewing gum or rocking in a chair treated as acceptable for a kinesthetic learner?
options: No — both are forbidden because they look informal
Yes — the lecture says it is acceptable while reading or studying
Only chewing is allowed; rocking is not
Only if the instructor has left the room
A.explain: Chewing gum, walking around, or rocking in a chair is acceptable while reading or studying.

A.q: What does the 'M' in SMART goals stand for?
options: Motivational
Measurable
Mandatory
Mysterious
A.explain: M = Measurable — you can count whether it happened.

A.q: The lecture compares a person without goals to which image?
options: A clock that never stops
A sheep in the pasture living from day to day
A mountain that cannot be climbed
A library with no books
A.explain: 'A person without goals is like a sheep out in the pasture just living from day to day.'

A.q: Short-term goals in this lecture are mainly:
options: Five-year career titles
Daily and weekly habits and assignments
Retirement plans
Other people's expectations
A.explain: Short-term goals are daily and weekly habits and assignments — the pyramid's foundation.

A.q: The opening quotation by J.C. Penney contrasts a stock clerk who has a goal with:
options: A stock clerk who has no goal
A professor who has no students
A student who has no textbooks
A clock with no hands
A.explain: 'Give me a stock clerk with a goal and I'll give you a man who will make history. Give me a man with no goals and I'll give you a stock clerk.'

A.q: For a goal to be realized, the lecture says you must develop:
options: Only a motivational quotation
An action plan and implementation intentions
A new personality
A promise with no calendar
A.explain: A goal needs an action plan and implementation intentions.

A.q: What does 'urgent' mean?
options: Tasks you can do anytime
Tasks for long-term goals
Tasks that require attention NOW
A.explain: Urgent means it requires attention NOW.

A.q: What is likely to happen when a person consistently neglects Quadrant II activities?
options: All tasks will become less important.
The person will eliminate interruptions permanently.
The person will have no need to prioritize tasks.
Important activities may become urgent crises in Quadrant I.
A.explain: Neglected QII items get promoted into Quadrant I as urgent crises.

A.q: Which outcome is a direct benefit of effective time management?
options: A guarantee that no urgent tasks will ever occur
Reduced anxiety through better preparation and prioritization
The ability to complete all tasks simultaneously
Elimination of every responsibility
A.explain: Better preparation and prioritization reduce anxiety.

A.q: Which items belong to Quadrant I (Urgent & Important)?
options: Trivia and busy work
Crisis, pressing problems, and deadline-driven projects critical to your strategic priorities
Some calls, some mails, and some meetings
Chatting and games
A.explain: QI: crisis, pressing problems, deadline-driven projects critical to strategic priorities.

A.q: Good time management helps you assign time to tasks:
options: Equally, regardless of the task
In the order the tasks arrive
In proportion to their importance — prioritizing
According to how enjoyable they are
A.explain: Assign time in proportion to importance — prioritizing.

A.q: A call interrupts your study session. It demands attention now, but it contributes nothing to your mission or values. Which quadrant does it belong to?
options: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
A.explain: Some calls and interruptions = urgent but not important = QIII.

A.q: Successful time management requires:
options: Expensive software and a private office
Permission from the dean
Self-evaluation and the desire to improve
A lighter course load
A.explain: Self-evaluation and the desire to improve.

A.q: Which of the following combinations is considered most readable for text?
options: Light font on a light background (e.g., yellow on white)
Dark font on a light background (e.g., blue on white)
Dark font on a dark background (e.g., black on navy)
A.explain: Dark font on light background gives the strongest, most readable contrast.

A.q: Which set of actions belongs to the PLAN stage?
options: Choosing fonts, checking spelling, thanking the audience
Setting your goal, collecting ideas and information, locating suitable resources, and knowing your audience beforehand
Scanning the audience's eyes and diversifying your voice
Handling nasty questions with humor
A.explain: Plan = goal + ideas + resources + knowing your audience beforehand.

A.q: Which rule matches the lecture's advice on animation?
options: Use a different noisy animation on every slide
The more animation, the better the talk
Do not use distracting animation, avoid noisy effects, do not go overboard — be consistent
Animation must never be used at all
A.explain: No distracting/noisy animation, don't overdo it, be consistent.

A.q: Why does the lecture recommend graphs rather than just tables and words?
options: Graphs take less time to draw
Data in graphs is easier to comprehend and retain, and trends are easier to visualize
Graphs do not need titles
Tables are forbidden in scientific talks
A.explain: Data in graphs is easier to comprehend and retain; trends are easier to visualize. Title every graph.

B.q: Which learning style primarily uses finger spelling?
options: Auditory
Kinesthetic
Non-Verbal – Visual
Verbal – Visual
B.explain: Finger spelling (tracing words with your finger to learn spelling) is listed among the KINESTHETIC study tools.

B.q: Which behavior is characteristic of a visual learner?
options: Avoiding all diagrams and charts
Absorbing spoken lectures without effort
Preferring to learn only through physical movement
Being distracted during lectures without visual aids
B.explain: Visual learners are easily distracted in lectures with no visual aids; absorbing spoken lectures effortlessly is auditory; movement-first is kinesthetic.

B.q: What should a kinesthetic learner do during a traditional lecture?
options: Avoid recording any information
Write out important facts
Use only unrelated background music
Listen without participating in any way
B.explain: During a traditional lecture, the kinesthetic learner should write out important facts.

B.q: A visual learner who hears a new concept typically does which of the following?
options: Stores the concept only as sound
Pictures the words and concepts as images
Must stand up before any encoding occurs
Ignores the spoken words completely
B.explain: Visual learners picture the words and concepts they hear as images.

B.q: How should a kinesthetic learner use flashcards, according to the lecture?
options: Avoid flashcards entirely
Read each card once and throw it away
Use flashcards and arrange them in groups to show relationships between ideas
Look at flashcards only from across the room
B.explain: Arrange flashcards in groups to show relationships between ideas — motion plus spatial structure.

B.q: What does the 'A' in SMART goals stand for?
options: Abstract
Ambitious
Action-Oriented (Attainable)
Automatic
B.explain: A = Action-Oriented (Attainable) — requires doing and can be reached.

B.q: In SMART goals, the letter S stands for:
options: Spontaneous
Specific
Seasonal
Silent
B.explain: S is Specific — 'Complete 33 credits by May', not 'do better'.

B.q: What happens once short-term goals are met, according to the pyramid slide?
options: Mid-range goals follow more easily
Long-term goals become unnecessary
You should stop writing new goals
Study hours can drop to zero
B.explain: Once short-term goals are met, mid-range goals follow more easily.

B.q: Which of the following is an example of a short-term academic block on the pyramid slide?
options: Owning a three-bedroom house with a pool
Create a study schedule and go to every class
Financial independence in late career
A dream job at a named salary only
B.explain: The foundation row: study schedule, every class, office hours, weekly reading, tutor, advisor.

B.q: An action plan should specify which four points?
options: Why other people should work, who to blame, which app to buy, and a motto
When, where, how, and for how long one is to act
Only the dream outcome and the feeling after success
The grade you want and nothing else
B.explain: When, where, how, and for how long — closing the door that time opens for distraction.

B.q: Which of the following means making a value judgment on each task you need to complete based on its worth and when it must be completed?
options: Scheduling
Planning
Priorities
B.explain: Priorities = a value judgment on each task by its worth and its deadline.

B.q: Which is the most appropriate first priority when several tasks compete for attention?
options: The task with the greatest value and the nearest deadline
The task that was assigned most recently
The easiest task, regardless of its importance
The task that is most enjoyable
B.explain: First priority = greatest value + nearest deadline.

B.q: A student wants to spend more time on important activities and reduce last-minute crises. Which strategy is best?
options: Focus mainly on interruptions because they are immediate
Plan important activities early and review them in a weekly schedule
Wait until tasks become urgent before starting them
B.explain: Plan important activities early and review them weekly — deliberate QII investment.

B.q: Which items belong to Quadrant II (Not urgent & Important)?
options: Preventing problems, strategy planning, relationship building, and recognizing new opportunities
Crisis management and deadline all-nighters
Interruptions and pressing matters
Trivia, busy work, and distractions
B.explain: QII: prevention, anticipation, strategy planning, relationship building, new opportunities.

B.q: Which of the following is listed as an early warning sign of time management problems?
options: Finishing every task before its deadline
Keeping a tidy weekly schedule
Asking teachers for extensions regularly
Sleeping eight hours a night
B.explain: Asking teachers for extensions regularly is on the warning-sign list.

B.q: You spend an afternoon creating next term's study strategy and building a relationship with a study partner. Nothing is due today. Which quadrant are you working in?
options: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
B.explain: Strategy planning + relationship building, no deadline = QII.

B.q: The conclusion warns that effective time management will require you to:
options: Do things you don't want to do when you don't want to do them — you have to push yourself
Wait until motivation arrives on its own
Study only your favorite subjects
Avoid every unpleasant task
B.explain: Do things you don't want to do when you don't want to do them — push yourself; the pay-off is always worth the effort.

B.q: Which of the following is a recommended way to end a presentation effectively?
options: Stop immediately when you run out of time.
End with a strong closing that summarizes key take-home messages.
Repeat the first slide to finish.
B.explain: End with a strong closing summarizing the key take-home messages — never end abruptly.

B.q: In the three-part organization, 'Tell them what you told them' is which part?
options: The opening
The message
The closing
The cover slide
B.explain: Closing = tell them what you told them.

B.q: According to the font guidance (Verdana), content text should be no smaller than:
options: 12 point
24 point
32 point
40 point
B.explain: Title ≈ 40 pt, bullets ≈ 32 pt, content no smaller than 24 pt.

B.q: In the faulty-graph example, which faults were called out?
options: Minor gridlines are unnecessary, the font is too small, colors are illogical, the title is missing, and shading is distracting
The graph had too few colors
Bars were used instead of lines
The graph was too small to see
B.explain: Unnecessary gridlines, too-small font, illogical colors, missing title, distracting shading.

C.q: Which learning style learns best by attending discussions and tutorials?
options: Visual
Auditory
Kinesthetic
C.explain: Auditory learners learn best by listening — discussions and tutorials deliver information as speech.

C.q: What is the main difference between verbal and non-verbal visual learners?
options: There is no difference between the two types
Verbal learners prefer movement, whereas non-verbal learners prefer sound
Verbal learners avoid reading, whereas non-verbal learners avoid images
Verbal visual learners prefer written information, whereas non-verbal visual learners prefer pictures
C.explain: Both use the visual channel. Verbal visual = written words; non-verbal visual = pictures.

C.q: Which strategy is recommended for kinesthetic learners when studying for extended periods?
options: Take frequent, short breaks
Remain completely still throughout study
Study continuously without moving
Avoid using flashcards
C.explain: Take frequent but not long breaks; arrange flashcards in groups.

C.q: Which classroom placement tip is given specifically to visual learners?
options: Sit at the back so the whole board is visible at once
Sit near the front of the classroom
Sit wherever the loudspeakers are strongest
Stand for the entire lecture
C.explain: Visual tips begin with: sit near the front of the classroom.

C.q: What is 'finger spelling' in the kinesthetic study tips?
options: Signing a full language instead of studying
Tracing words with your finger to learn spelling
Typing without looking at the keys
Asking someone else to write for you
C.explain: Trace words with your finger to learn spelling — a kinesthetic tool.

C.q: What does the 'R' in SMART goals stand for?
options: Rigid
Realistic (Relevant)
Random
Reserved
C.explain: R = Realistic (Relevant) — fits your life and matters to your values.

C.q: In SMART goals, the letter M stands for:
options: Motivational
Mysterious
Measurable
Maximum
C.explain: M is Measurable — credits, GPA, hours studied.

C.q: Which hint is given for keeping goals visible?
options: Keep them only in your head so they stay private
Write them down and put them where you will see them every day
Tell no one and review them once a year
Write them on an exam script only
C.explain: Write goals down and put them where you will see them every day.

C.q: As the semester or year ends, what should happen to short-term and mid-range goals?
options: They should be frozen forever
They should be replaced with new ones
They should be deleted and never rewritten
They should be converted into quotes only
C.explain: Replace short-term and mid-range goals with new ones; the long-term peak can remain.

C.q: In Pham and Taylor (1999), students who focused mental simulation on the outcome (seeing the high grade and the feeling) tended to:
options: Study more and earn better grades
Study less and earn poorer grades
Need no action plan at all
Sleep through the midterm with no cost
C.explain: The outcome group studied less and earned poorer grades — fantasy of the trophy is not rehearsal of the work.

C.q: Which of the following is known as the enemy of time management?
options: Setting goals
Procrastination
Prioritizing tasks
C.explain: Procrastination is the enemy of time management.

C.q: Which combination represents the three key steps to good time management?
options: Hourly meetings, continuous messaging, and task avoidance
Daily exercise, social media review, and spontaneous planning
Weekly schedule, daily to-do-list, and long-term planning
Crisis response, multitasking, and delaying difficult tasks
C.explain: Weekly schedule + daily to-do list + long-term planning.

C.q: Which statement best defines Time Management in this lecture?
options: A natural talent that some people are born with
The number of hours a student spends studying each week
A method of avoiding all urgent tasks
The development of processes and tools that increase efficiency and productivity
C.explain: TM = development of processes and tools that increase efficiency and productivity.

C.q: Which items belong to Quadrant III (Urgent & Not important)?
options: Interruptions, some calls, some mails, some reports, some meetings, and pressing matters
Strategy planning and relationship building
Deadline-driven projects on your strategic priorities
Anticipating future activities
C.explain: QIII: interruptions, some calls/mails/reports/meetings, pressing matters.

C.q: 'Your grades don't reflect your ability' is presented in the lecture as:
options: An early warning sign of time management problems
Proof that the examinations were unfair
A reason to change majors immediately
A rule about fixed intelligence
C.explain: It is an early warning sign — the remedy starts with completing the Time Management Matrix.

C.q: Two hours disappear into trivia, busy work, and chatting-and-games time wasters. Which quadrant absorbed the time?
options: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
C.explain: Trivia, busy work, chatting and games = QIV.

C.q: Which early warning sign of TM problems involves the quality of submitted work?
options: Submitting work that is not up to your usual standard
Attending every lecture on time
Finishing tasks early
Keeping every commitment in a calendar
C.explain: Submitting work below your usual standard is a listed warning sign.

C.q: Which statement best defines a presentation, as given in this lecture?
options: A written exam paper submitted for grading
An informal chat between classmates about a lecture
A process of communicating knowledge, thoughts, ideas, and/or research results to specific audiences
A printed handout distributed after class
C.explain: A presentation communicates knowledge, thoughts, ideas, and/or research results to specific audiences.

C.q: What should the OPENING of your talk do, according to the organization rule?
options: Tell them what you are going to say
Tell them what you told them
Invite nasty questions
Show the conclusion graph
C.explain: Opening = tell them what you are going to say.

C.q: Which fonts are named as standard, readable choices for slides?
options: Garamond Italic, Gill Sans Condensed, and Century Gothic
Decorative script fonts
Any font smaller than 12 point
Times New Roman, Tahoma, Verdana, or Arial
C.explain: Times New Roman, Tahoma, Verdana, or Arial.

C.q: About spelling and syntax, the lecture advises you to:
options: Trust the audience to correct your spelling
Check spelling only after the presentation
Proofread your presentation before they see it — and asking a friend for help is OK
Ignore spelling because content matters more
C.explain: Proofread before they see it — asking a friend for help is OK.

D.q: A student who prefers to see information presented in the form of pictures, diagrams, cartoons, or demonstrations is best described as having which type of learning style?
options: Visual
Auditory
Kinesthetic
D.explain: Preferring pictures, diagrams, cartoons, or demonstrations defines a visual learner.

D.q: Which study strategy is especially appropriate for a visual learner?
options: Listen to lectures without looking at any materials
Use charts, maps, notes, and flashcards
Study only by walking around
Avoid writing down key ideas
D.explain: Charts, maps, notes, and flashcards are core visual study tools; also sit near the front and use highlighters.

D.q: Which statement best reflects the lecture's conclusion about learning styles?
options: Learners should be flexible and adapt to different styles
Each person is purely one learning style
Learning styles cannot change or overlap
Learners should use only their preferred style
D.explain: Be flexible and adapt to different styles as much as you can.

D.q: Which of the following is a listed study tip for visual learners?
options: Color things and use highlighter pens
Avoid all written notes
Study only with loud background speech
Never draw a concept
D.explain: Coloring, highlighters, drawing concepts, and writing key words are visual tips.

D.q: The handout points to which questionnaire as the practical inventory?
options: A personality test that ignores sensory channels
The Visual, Aural, Read/Write, Kinesthetic (VARK) questionnaire
A one-question 'are you smart?' survey
An athletic fitness inventory
D.explain: The VARK questionnaire (Visual, Aural, Read/Write, Kinesthetic) at vark-learn.com.

D.q: What does the 'T' in SMART goals stand for?
options: Temporary
Theoretical
Trendy
Time-bound
D.explain: T = Time-bound — a deadline exists.

D.q: In this lecture's SMART list, A stands for Action-oriented, which is also glossed as:
options: Abstract
Automatic
Attainable
Avoidant
D.explain: A is Action-Oriented, with Attainable in parentheses.

D.q: If a short-term goal is not working, the lecture says you should:
options: Abandon the long-term goal immediately
Change the short-term goal
Study in one 12-hour marathon to force it
Ignore the problem until the year ends
D.explain: Change short-term goals if they are not working — the peak stays, the weekly block is redesigned.

D.q: Dr. Boyce Watkins is quoted as saying the path to greatness is usually paved with:
options: Perfect first attempts
Failure, after trying over and over again
A single lucky weekend
Avoiding all feedback
D.explain: 'The path to greatness is usually paved with failure' — most big successes come after repeated failure.

D.q: In the same study, students who focused mental simulation on the process (seeing themselves actually studying) tended to:
options: Study more and earn better grades
Abandon the midterm
Need more outcome daydreaming
Perform worse than the outcome group
D.explain: The process group studied more and earned better grades — picture the work, not the trophy.

D.q: Which statement best defines time management?
options: Completing as many tasks as possible without planning
Developing processes and tools to improve efficiency and productivity
Using every available hour for academic work
Avoiding all activities that require immediate attention
D.explain: Time management = developing processes and tools that increase efficiency and productivity.

D.q: What is the primary purpose of developing a weekly schedule?
options: To replace the need for daily planning
To ensure every minute is spent working
To provide an overview of committed time and available time
To record only tasks that were not completed
D.explain: A weekly schedule shows committed time against available time.

D.q: Time management is also defined as the ability to:
options: Work only on the tasks you enjoy most
Get things done when they should be done
Memorize the college timetable
Avoid deadlines by renegotiating them
D.explain: Get things done when they should be done — right task, right time.

D.q: Which items belong to Quadrant IV (Not urgent & Not important)?
options: Crisis and pressing problems
Relationship building
Trivia, busy work, distractions, and time wasters such as chatting and games
Preventing future problems
D.explain: QIV: trivia, busy work, distractions, time wasters (chatting and games).

D.q: Procrastination may give immediate satisfaction, but the lecture says it brings:
options: Anxiety, reduced sleep, illness, lower grades, poorer quality of work, less learning from being rushed, and a personal sense of disappointment
Better learning through last-minute focus
More free time and higher-quality work
Stronger relationships with instructors
D.explain: The full bill: anxiety, reduced sleep, illness, lower grades, poorer work, less learning, disappointment.

D.q: In the practical task, a person works 42 hours a week and spends 21 of those hours on urgent and important work. What share of the workweek is that?
D.explain: 21 of 42 hours = 50% in Quadrant I.

D.q: Which warning sign involves sacrificing things you like?
options: Reading for pleasure on weekends
Joining a study group
Sleeping early before exams
Having to let go of activities you enjoy because of a lack of time or low grades
D.explain: Letting go of activities you enjoy due to lack of time or low grades is a warning sign.

D.q: The 'presentation circuit' consists of which four components?
options: Presenter, audience, message, and setting/context
Slides, projector, podium, and microphone
Title, outline, body, and references
Writer, editor, reviewer, and publisher
D.explain: Presenter and audience around a message, all inside a setting/context.

D.q: The first slide of a presentation must contain:
options: The complete text of the talk
The title of the presentation and your name, position, and affiliation
Only the institution logo
The list of references
D.explain: Title + name, position, and affiliation (± date, institution logo).

D.q: Why should you NOT use all capital letters?
options: Capital letters are not allowed by the software
It shortens the presentation
It makes text hard to read, conceals acronyms, and denies capitals for EMPHASIS
It only affects the footer
D.explain: ALL CAPS is hard to read, conceals acronyms, and denies capitals for emphasis.

D.q: Why does the lecture insist on an effective and strong closing?
options: It reduces the number of slides
Your audience is likely to remember your last words
It prevents the audience from asking questions
It replaces the outline slide
D.explain: The audience is likely to remember your last words — take-home messages, no abrupt ending.

E.q: Which statement best defines learning styles?
options: The subjects students choose to study
The grades students receive in examinations
The length of time required to complete a course
The processes and techniques people use to learn
E.explain: Learning styles are the processes and techniques people use to learn things (facts, skills, attitudes).

E.q: Which characteristic is most typical of an auditory learner?
options: Preferring diagrams over all spoken explanations
Preferring to hear information spoken
Remembering information only as written words
Learning primarily through touching objects
E.explain: Auditory learners prefer to hear information spoken and can often absorb a lecture with little effort.

E.q: Which statement about learners and learning styles is accurate?
options: Every learner has only one permanent style
Learners cannot benefit from different approaches
Most learners are mixed rather than purely one style
Learning style is unrelated to learning preferences
E.explain: No one is purely one style — learners are mixed.

E.q: Which auditory characteristic is easy to confuse with inattention?
options: Preferring maps over speech
Often avoiding eye contact in order to concentrate
Needing intense visual slides in every minute of class
Refusing to join any spoken activity
E.explain: Auditory learners often avoid eye contact to concentrate — easily mistaken for rudeness or inattention.

E.q: 'Something you want to achieve' is the definition of which of the following?
options: Habit
Plan
Goal
Challenge
E.explain: A goal is something you want to achieve; a habit is repeated behaviour, a plan is the route, a challenge is an obstacle.

E.q: Which statement best defines goals in this lecture?
options: Vague wishes about the distant future
Well-defined plans aimed at achieving a specific result
Grades awarded by an examiner
The subjects a student is forced to take
E.explain: Goals are well-defined plans aimed at achieving a specific result.

E.q: In this lecture's SMART list, R stands for Realistic, which is also glossed as:
options: Random
Relevant
Rigid
Rare
E.explain: R is Realistic, with Relevant in parentheses.

E.q: Which statement matches the lecture's advice on how high to aim?
options: Aim far below what you can do so you never miss
Be realistic but aim higher than you think you can achieve
Aim only at what is already finished
Never write a number in a goal
E.explain: Be realistic but aim higher than you think you can achieve.

E.q: Which morning habit is listed first among the powerful habits?
options: Get up at a different time each day to stay flexible
Get up at the same time every morning
Sleep until noon if the night was long
Skip mornings and study only after 10:00 p.m.
E.explain: Get up at the same time every morning, then keep a regular schedule.

E.q: Keeping track of progress is described as which personal task?
options: Self-regulation — monitor progress and modify the plan as necessary
Waiting for the college to monitor you
Checking social media for motivation only
Rewriting the long-term goal every hour
E.explain: Self-regulation: monitor progress, modify the plan, set intermediate milestones, keep a timetable.

E.q: Which statement best distinguishes an urgent activity from an important activity?
options: Urgent activities are enjoyable, while important activities are difficult.
Urgent activities are always important, and important activities are never urgent.
Urgent activities require immediate attention, while important activities contribute to priorities and values.
Urgent activities are long-term goals, while important activities are interruptions.
E.explain: Urgent = immediate attention (a timing claim); important = contributes to priorities and values (a mission claim).

E.q: What behavior is an early warning sign of time-management problems?
options: Frequently asking teachers for extensions
Using a long-term plan to organize future work
Completing important tasks before their deadlines
Preparing a weekly schedule in advance
E.explain: Regularly asking for extensions is an early warning sign.

E.q: What does the lecture say about how time management develops?
options: It is a skill that must be worked on, and most people find it a life-long challenge
It just happens naturally with age
It can be installed once and then forgotten
It is fixed at the same level for everyone
E.explain: It is a skill that must be worked on — a life-long challenge for most people.

E.q: Which quadrant does the lecture call 'the heart of the personal quality management'?
options: Quadrant I — Urgent & Important
Quadrant II — Not urgent & Important
Quadrant III — Urgent & Not important
Quadrant IV — Not urgent & Not important
E.explain: Quadrant II is 'the heart of the personal quality management'.

E.q: Setting priorities means making a value judgment on each task based on:
options: Its length and its difficulty
The mood you are in that day
The alphabetical order of the task
Its worth and when it must be completed
E.explain: Worth and when it must be completed.

E.q: In the practical task, after listing your weekly tasks in the 'Urgent & Important' matrix, what are you asked to do?
options: Hide the matrix from your colleagues
Put the first things first, then share and discuss with the colleague beside you
Delete every Quadrant I task
Convert the matrix into an essay
E.explain: Put first things first, then share and discuss with the colleague beside you.

E.q: The lecture asks how urgent activities can take us away from:
options: Activities that enable us to carry out our mission or vision
Sleep and meals only
Social media and games
Nothing — urgency is always useful
E.explain: Urgent activities steal time from mission- and vision-carrying activities.

E.q: According to the introduction, which tasks require the ability to write scientifically and professionally?
options: Only multiple-choice examinations
Assignments, research activities, scientific reports, and dissertations
Social media posts only
None — writing is not needed after admission
E.explain: Assignments, research activities, scientific reports, dissertations.

E.q: Your second slide should list:
options: Every reference in full detail
The thank-you message
Complete paragraphs of the introduction
The objectives, agenda, or outline of your talk — main points only
E.explain: Objectives/agenda — main points only; follow that order for the rest of the talk.

E.q: According to the lecture, italics are properly used for:
options: Every bullet point
Quotes, highlighting thoughts or ideas, and titles of books, journals, or magazines
All headings and nothing else
Numbers only
E.explain: Quotes, highlighted thoughts/ideas, and book/journal/magazine titles.

E.q: What is the purpose of the 'Questions' slide at the end of a presentation?
options: Invite your audience to ask questions
List the references
Show the title again
Announce the next lecture
E.explain: Invite your audience to ask questions — and handle them well.

F.q: Which factors are included in a learner's learning style?
options: Financial, social, and occupational factors
Physical, chemical, and environmental factors
Cognitive, affective, and physiological factors
Academic, athletic, and artistic factors only
F.explain: A learning style encompasses cognitive, affective, and physiological factors — how a learner perceives, interacts with, and responds to the learning environment.

F.q: Which study strategy is recommended for an auditory learner?
options: Study only by drawing maps
Read study material aloud
Avoid discussions and tutorials
Use pictures without verbal explanation
F.explain: Read assignments, directions, and new material out loud; record and replay; have test questions read aloud.

F.q: A student remembers information as clear pictures and benefits from videos, maps, and diagrams. Which type of learner is most likely?
options: Verbal visual learner
Non-verbal visual learner
Kinesthetic learner
Auditory learner
F.explain: Picture format + remembering clear pictures = non-verbal visual learner.

F.q: Which statement about notes is most true of many auditory learners?
options: They must copy every slide word for word or they learn nothing
They may not need careful notes to learn from a spoken lecture
They cannot learn unless the page is full of diagrams
They should never listen to a recording of the class
F.explain: Auditory learners can absorb a lecture with little effort and may not need careful notes.

F.q: Which of the following is a goal with an outcome that is based on a specific date / time?
options: Fixed goals
Flexible goals
Condensed goals
F.explain: A fixed goal's outcome is based on a specific date or time — a set deadline.

F.q: Besides being plans, goals are described as which of the following?
options: Roadmaps for achieving what you want in life
Substitutes for attending class
Guarantees of a high Grade Point Average (GPA)
Personality types that cannot change
F.explain: Goals are roadmaps for achieving what you want in life — a course of action you intend to pursue.

F.q: In SMART goals, the letter T stands for:
options: Theoretical
Time-bound
Temporary only
Team-based
F.explain: T is Time-bound — a deadline turns a wish into a schedule.

F.q: 'Make sure you understand the price of reaching your goals' means you should:
options: Ignore the cost and hope luck pays it
Know what time, effort, and trade-offs the goal will require
Pay someone else to hold the goal
Treat money as the only price that exists
F.explain: Every goal has a price in hours, sleep, social time, and attention.

F.q: Which tracking tool is recommended for assignments and appointments?
options: Memory alone
A to-do list or appointment calendar
A motivational poster with no dates
Someone else's timetable only
F.explain: Use a to-do list or appointment calendar for assignments and appointments.

F.q: Which statement best captures the difference between outcome simulation and process simulation?
options: Outcome simulation pictures the high grade and the feeling; process simulation pictures the studying that would produce that grade
They are identical exercises with different titles
Process simulation is only about buying stationery
Outcome simulation always produces more study hours
F.explain: Outcome = grade + feeling; process = the studying that leads to that grade. Only the second trained behavior.

F.q: A critical assignment due today has a major effect on a student's academic progress. In which quadrant should it be placed?
options: Quadrant I: Urgent and Important
Quadrant IV: Not Urgent and Not Important
Quadrant III: Urgent and Not Important
Quadrant II: Not Urgent and Important
F.explain: Due today = urgent; major effect on progress = important → Quadrant I.

F.q: What is likely a consequence of procrastinating on an important academic task?
options: More sleep and improved learning
Increased anxiety and poorer-quality work
Lower stress without any disadvantages
More time for completing the task carefully
F.explain: Procrastination → increased anxiety and poorer-quality work.

F.q: In the matrix, 'urgent' activities are those requiring:
options: Careful long-term planning
Permission from a supervisor
Immediate attention — NOW
A written budget first
F.explain: Urgent = immediate attention — NOW.

F.q: To lead effectively, the lecture says you need to spend more time in:
options: Quadrant I, personally handling every crisis
Quadrant II — Important but not Urgent
Quadrant III, answering every interruption
Quadrant IV, recovering from the week
F.explain: Spend more time in Quadrant II — Important but not Urgent.

F.q: According to the lecture, which tasks should be your #1 priority?
options: The tasks you enjoy most
The easiest tasks, to build momentum
The tasks that are worth the most and due the soonest
The tasks your friends are working on
F.explain: Worth the most + due the soonest = #1 priority.

F.q: What is the stated purpose of writing a daily to-do list?
options: To provide daily reminders to assure key tasks are not forgotten
To rank classmates by their grades
To replace the weekly schedule entirely
To record dreams and moods
F.explain: Daily reminders so key tasks are not forgotten.

F.q: In the lecture's own words, procrastination is:
options: A harmless habit
A modern study technique
The enemy of time management
The key to creativity
F.explain: 'Procrastination: Enemy of Time Management.'

F.q: The lecture describes a successful person as one who is capable of:
options: Speaking without stopping for a full hour
Memorizing every slide word for word
Avoiding the audience's eyes
Communicating his knowledge, experiences, and thoughts in a professional manner
F.explain: Communicating knowledge, experiences, and thoughts in a professional manner.

F.q: The recommended slide count is:
options: 1–2 slides per minute of your presentation
1–2 slides for the whole presentation
10 slides per minute
As many slides as the file can hold
F.explain: 1–2 slides per minute.

F.q: Which rule governs font color?
options: Use a different color for each point or word
Use bright colors on a white background
Match the font color to the background exactly
Use a font color that contrasts sharply with the background
F.explain: Contrast sharply with the background — dark font on light background.

F.q: 'The mind… starts working the minute you're born, and never stops until you get up to speak' humorously refers to:
options: Audience boredom
Writer's block during essays
Presentation phobia
Time management failure
F.explain: Presentation phobia — which can be healthy or unhealthy.

G.q: Why is it important for learners to know their own learning style?
options: It determines their final examination grade
It eliminates the need to attend classes
It guarantees that they will use only one learning method
It helps them seek learning situations that suit them
G.explain: Knowing your style lets you seek situations and experiences that meet that style.

G.q: Which activity is particularly suitable for supporting an auditory learner?
options: Studying without any discussion
Joining a study group
Replacing all spoken material with diagrams
Avoiding tutorials
G.explain: Join a study group, work with a study buddy, and attend discussions and tutorials — spoken, social channels.

G.q: A student prefers textbooks and written outlines and remembers written information mentally. Which type of learner is most likely?
options: Verbal visual learner
Auditory learner
Non-verbal visual learner
Kinesthetic learner
G.explain: Written format + remembering written words in the mind's eye = verbal visual learner.

G.q: Which extra check does the lecture recommend for auditory learners?
options: Have your hearing checked on a regular basis
Have your color vision checked every week
Avoid sitting where you can hear
Refuse all background music
G.explain: Sit where you can hear, and have your hearing checked regularly.

G.q: What type of goal is usually achieved over a period of 5 years?
options: Short-term goal
Daily goal
Long-term goal
G.explain: A long-term goal is usually achieved over about 5 years.

G.q: What do goals reflect, according to the lecture?
options: Only the college timetable
Only what other people expect
Your values and your priorities
Random interest with no hierarchy
G.explain: Goals reflect your values and your priorities.

G.q: The lecture compares achieving a long-term goal to:
options: Winning a single lottery ticket
Building a pyramid
Waiting for motivation to arrive
Memorizing one quotation
G.explain: Achieving a long-term goal is like building a pyramid: short-term base, medium middle, long-term peak.

G.q: What should you do with obstacles to a five-year goal?
options: Pretend they do not exist
Recognize them, judge how much control you have, then avoid or eliminate them
List them once and never look again
Treat every obstacle as fate
G.explain: Recognize obstacles, judge how much control you have, then avoid or eliminate them.

G.q: Which human-contact habits are listed as supports for reaching goals?
options: Avoid all instructors until the final exam
Find a study partner, use office hours, attend study-skills class, and meet the instructor after the first exam
Only message classmates the night before the test
Never form a study group
G.explain: Study partner, office hours, study-skills class, and meeting the instructor after the first exam.

G.q: On the later 'life pyramid' slide, which sequence shows goals building toward the next?
options: Dream house first, then a degree, then waking up
Bachelor's degree with a target Grade Point Average (GPA), then a job, then financial independence and family goals
Marriage first with no education block
A pool with no income plan
G.explain: Degree with target GPA → dream job → financial independence, with family goals on the map — lower blocks hold higher ones.

G.q: Which activity is the best example of Quadrant II: Not Urgent and Important?
options: Playing games during scheduled study time
Responding to a crisis that requires immediate action
Planning a study schedule before examinations begin
Answering an unimportant interruption immediately
G.explain: Planning before exams is important but not pressing today — the classic Quadrant II activity.

G.q: Which task belongs in Quadrant III: Urgent and Not Important?
options: Preparing a long-term study strategy
Completing a critical assignment due today
An interruption that demands immediate attention but does not support major priorities
Playing a game when there is no deadline or benefit
G.explain: QIII = urgent but does not support major priorities — the classic interruption.

G.q: In the matrix, 'important' activities are those that:
options: Are the loudest and most visible
Appear at the top of an inbox
Can be delegated to anyone
Contribute to your mission, values, and priorities
G.explain: Important = contributes to your mission, values, and priorities.

G.q: According to the lecture, what happens when you do not spend enough time in Quadrant II?
options: Your mission and values change automatically
Many items move over into Quadrant I, and you are constantly handling crises
Quadrant IV items disappear
Every task becomes enjoyable
G.explain: Items move into Quadrant I and you are constantly handling crises.

G.q: Which of the following are the three key steps to good time management?
options: Cramming, napping, and repeating
Developing a weekly schedule, writing a daily to-do list, and preparing a long-term plan
Working harder, sleeping less, and skipping meals
Memorizing, highlighting, and rereading
G.explain: Weekly schedule, daily to-do list, long-term plan.

G.q: What is the stated purpose of preparing a long-term plan?
options: To memorize dates for a history exam
To replace the daily to-do list entirely
To avoid ever planning the week
To promote overall organization and future planning
G.explain: Promotes overall organization and future planning.

G.q: According to the benefits list, good time management makes you:
options: A more productive, successful person with a more balanced life
Isolated from friends and family
Dependent on your instructor
Immune to deadlines
G.explain: A more productive, successful person with a more balanced life.

G.q: What are the 3 P's of presentation?
options: Plan, Prepare, Present
Practice, Perform, Publish
Plan, Print, Prove
Prepare, Pause, Perfect
G.explain: Plan, Prepare, Present.

G.q: Good slide structure means writing:
options: Complete sentences with as many words as possible
Full paragraphs copied from the textbook
In point form — key words and phrases only, 4–5 points per slide
At least 12 points per slide
G.explain: Point form, 4–5 points per slide, key words only — avoid wordiness.

G.q: What is advised about presentation backgrounds?
options: Use light backgrounds and keep the same background consistently throughout
Use dark, busy backgrounds for drama
Change the background on every slide to keep attention
Background choice does not affect readability
G.explain: Light backgrounds, same background consistently throughout.

G.q: Complete the lecture's key sentence about delivery: 'It is not WHAT we say, but…'
options: …how long we speak
…HOW we say it
…how many slides we show
…how loudly we apologize
G.explain: It is not WHAT we say, but HOW we say it.

H.q: Why is it useful for teachers to understand the learning styles of others?
options: It allows them to replace all classroom activities
It allows them to avoid using teaching aids
It helps them teach and work in groups more effectively
It proves that all learners learn identically
H.explain: Knowing how others learn helps you teach them and work in groups more effectively.

H.q: Which learning style prefers touch and motion as primary ways of taking in information?
options: Visual
Verbal visual
Auditory
Kinesthetic
H.explain: Kinesthetic learners prefer touch and motion as the primary mode for taking in information.

H.q: Which tool was recommended in the lecture for discovering one's learning style?
options: Physical fitness assessment
Handwriting speed test
Personality-free examination
Learning Styles Inventory
H.explain: Discover your style by completing the Learning Styles Inventory.

H.q: Which set of motions does the lecture associate with kinesthetic learning?
options: Only silent reading in a locked chair
Jittering, walking, yo-yoing, chewing, coloring, typing, writing
Listening with eyes closed and hands still
Watching a diagram without touching anything
H.explain: Kinesthetic learners learn better while jittering, walking, yo-yoing, chewing, coloring, typing, or writing.

H.q: What does the 'S' in SMART goals stand for?
options: Specific
Significant
Strategic
H.explain: S = Specific — a named target, not a vague wish.

H.q: A plan for where you want to be five years from now is classified as a:
options: Short-term goal
Medium-range goal
Long-term goal
Daily habit only
H.explain: The five-year plan is a long-term goal — 'Five years from now, I will be…'

H.q: In the goal pyramid, medium-range goals sit at approximately which horizon?
options: Today only
1–2 years from now
10–20 years from now
The next 20 minutes
H.explain: Medium-range = 1–2 years; long-term ≈ 5 years; short-term = daily and weekly.

H.q: Which study-habit cluster is listed as a powerful way to reach academic goals?
options: One monthly marathon, starting after midnight, with no calendar
20–25 hours a week outside class, in small bits of time, with most studying done before 10:00 p.m.
Zero hours outside class if the lecture was attended
Only group work after 1:00 a.m.
H.explain: 20–25 hours a week outside class, in small bits, most studying done before 10:00 p.m.

H.q: Why meet the instructor after the first exam?
options: To argue the grade with no plan to change anything
To learn from mistakes and get feedback
To cancel the rest of the semester
To replace the long-term goal with a complaint
H.explain: To learn from mistakes and get feedback.

H.q: Which quadrant has tasks that are Not Urgent and Important?
options: Quadrant 1
Quadrant 2
Quadrant 3
H.explain: Quadrant 2 = Not Urgent + Important — planning, prevention, preparation.

H.q: Why is Quadrant II described as the heart of personal quality management?
options: It consists mainly of entertainment and time-wasting activities.
It allows people to avoid all responsibilities.
It contains all urgent crises that must be solved immediately.
It focuses on planning, capacity development, prevention, and preparation.
H.explain: Quadrant II focuses on planning, capacity development, prevention, and preparation.

H.q: Which activity is the clearest example of Quadrant IV: Not Urgent and Not Important?
options: Preventing future academic problems through planning
Completing a high-value task due today
Responding to a serious emergency
Spending study time on games and unnecessary chatting
H.explain: Games and unnecessary chatting = neither deadline nor payoff = QIV.

H.q: If an activity is urgent, does that automatically mean it is important?
options: Yes — urgency always proves importance
Only if a teacher assigned it
No — an activity can be urgent yet contribute nothing to your mission
Only during examination weeks
H.explain: No — urgency is a timing claim; importance is a mission claim.

H.q: Which benefit of good time management is stated in the lecture?
options: It guarantees top grades without effort
It removes every source of stress from life
It makes you better prepared for the demands of your life — therefore decreasing anxiety
It shortens the semester
H.explain: Better prepared for life's demands → decreases anxiety.

H.q: What is the stated purpose of developing a weekly schedule?
options: To provide an overview of free and committed time
To record the grades of every quiz
To list the phone numbers of classmates
To track how much money is spent
H.explain: An overview of free and committed time.

H.q: According to the conclusion, time management is a skill that:
options: Only students need
Only managers need
Everyone must work on in all areas of their life — personal, academic, and work
Talented people can safely skip
H.explain: Everyone must work on it — personal, academic, and work.

H.q: What should the first slide of a presentation typically include?
options: Only the title of the presentation
Title, your name, position, affiliation, and optionally additional information such as date or institution logo
Only detailed content of the presentation
H.explain: Cover slide: title + name, position, affiliation (± date, institution logo) — not detailed content.

H.q: The reminder 'A person who is going nowhere normally gets there' is attached to which planning step?
options: Locating the suitable resources
Collecting ideas and information
Setting your goal
Designing the background colors
H.explain: It hangs under 'Set Your Goal'.

H.q: Why does the lecture recommend showing one point at a time?
options: It makes the slide file smaller
It helps the audience concentrate, prevents them from reading ahead, and keeps your talk focused
It hides weak points from the audience
It is required by all presentation software
H.explain: Helps concentration, prevents reading ahead, keeps the talk focused.

H.q: Which combination appears on the lecture's 'avoid such combinations' list?
options: Dark blue on white
Black on light grey
Green on blue (also dark yellow on green, purple on blue, orange on green, red on green)
A dark font on a light background
H.explain: Avoid green on blue, dark yellow on green, purple on blue, orange on green, red on green — and bright colors on white.

H.q: Which treatment does the lecture give for presentation phobia?
options: Practice, practice, practice — using colleagues, friends, or relatives as audiences — and take a couple of deep breaths before standing up
Avoid all presentations for a year
Speak only to mirrors, never to live audiences
Read slides word-for-word to avoid mistakes
H.explain: Practice repeatedly with friendly audiences + deep breaths before standing up.
